title: Cacio e Pepe
subtitle: Roman pasta with pecorino and black pepper
excerpt: The Roman pasta of three ingredients: spaghetti, aged pecorino, and an abundance of coarsely ground black pepper, bound together by the starchy pasta water into a silky, intensely savoury sauce. A masterclass in technique over ingredients.

recipe.sourceNotes: Cacio e pepe (cheese and pepper) is one of the four canonical Roman pasta dishes, alongside amatriciana, carbonara, and gricia. It is considered the most technically demanding of the four despite having the fewest ingredients: three, at their simplest. The sauce is an emulsion of finely grated pecorino romano and starchy pasta cooking water, seasoned with a large amount of coarsely ground black pepper that has been toasted in the pan. The challenge is temperature control: too hot and the cheese seizes into clumps rather than melting into a sauce; too little pasta water and the sauce is dry; too much and it is thin and watery. The technique requires practice: the pasta must be added off the heat, with the cheese and water introduced slowly while tossing continuously. Pecorino romano (not the milder pecorino sardo or parmesan) is the traditional cheese; a 50/50 blend with parmesan produces a slightly milder result that many find more accessible.

content.text: Grate the cheese as finely as possible; coarse grating produces lumps that will not melt smoothly. Use significantly less water than usual to cook the pasta so the starch concentration is much higher: this is the secret to the emulsion. Remove the pan from the heat entirely before adding the cheese; residual heat alone should melt it. Work quickly and keep tossing.

items.preparation: finely grated; use pecorino romano if available, or half and half with parmesan
coarsely ground; toast in a dry pan first

content.text: Coarsely grind the black pepper. Toast it in a large dry frying pan over medium heat for 60 seconds until fragrant, shaking the pan. Add 1 ladle of pasta cooking water to the pan and let it simmer for 30 seconds; this creates the pepper base. Remove from the heat.

Cook the pasta in salted water using about half the usual amount of water so the starch concentration is high. Cook until 1 minute before al dente. Reserve 400 ml of the cooking water before draining. Drain the pasta.

Add the pasta to the pan with the pepper. Add a ladleful of pasta water and toss over medium heat for 1 minute. Remove from the heat completely. Add the grated cheese in two additions, tossing vigorously and adding pasta water a splash at a time to create a smooth, glossy sauce. The cheese should melt fully into a cream; if it clumps, add more water and toss. Serve immediately.
